newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fischler to seek extra BSE food safety rules.
newsitem.headline: Fischler to seek extra BSE food safety rules.

text.p: Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler is due on Wednesday to call for further measures to protect consumers against mad cow disease, including banning exports of British gelatine and risky cattle and sheep offal.

A Commission spokesman said it will be asked to approve, at a meeting in Strasbourg, action guidelines which would then be discussed by the Standing Veterinary Committee of senior member state officials.
If there is a qualified majority in favour of the measures, they could then be approved by the European Commission. If not, the issues would be referred to EU farm ministers.
"It's unclear how long it will be before any decisions are taken," the spokesman said.
The report will be presented by Fischler because it concerns legislative measures, rather than food safety inspections and scientific advice which are handled by Emma Bonino, officials explained.
Bonino has been pushing for speedy implementation of advice given on April 3 by the multidisciplinary scientific committee raising doubts about the safety of gelatine made from British cattle.

The EU banned British gelatine exports in March 1996 as part of a worldwide embargo on British beef triggered by London's admission of a link between mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), and a human equivalent, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD).

Although in June 1996 the European Commission eased the ban on gelatine made from British beef, it has not approved any such exports because British manufacturers failed to meet the strict heat processing pre-conditions.
Britain's four gelatine producers considered that the terms were so severe that they made production uneconomic. Instead they turned to beef raw materials from other countries.
Officials stressed that the draft gelatine ban was only part of a series of measures to tighten up BSE controls.

They said that pressure for extra food safety measures had grown following recent EU inspections showing that member states have not been respecting rules on the disposal of cattle and sheep offal. A number of member states could be taken to court.
The New Scientist magazine reported this month that BSE may be silently spreading across Europe because farmers and veterinarians were failing to report sick cows.
Fischler is expected to make a fresh bid to ban specified risk material from cattle and sheep -- brains, eyes, spinal cord and spleen -- from human and animal food.

In December, EU farm ministers rejected the proposal arguing that it was unnecessary and economically excessive as their countries were virtually free of BSE and scrapie, a similar brain-wasting disease in sheep.
Infected meat and bonemeal mixed into cattle and sheep feed is believed to be the main cause of BSE.
